### Supporting basis

C++ `std::sort` is highly optimized, typically implementing IntroSort, which combines QuickSort, HeapSort, and InsertionSort. It dynamically switches algorithms to guarantee O(n log n) worst-case performance, protecting against pathological inputs that degrade naive QuickSort to O(n^2). For 10 million `double` values, memory access patterns and cache efficiency are critical. Library implementations are tuned by CPU architecture experts, offering superior branch prediction and instruction utilization. A custom QuickSort often lacks these low-level optimizations, random pivot selection robustness, and tail-recursion elimination. Furthermore, `std::sort` handles edge cases and partial sorting efficiently. Writing a custom sort introduces maintenance overhead and potential bugs without guaranteeing performance gains. Benchmarks consistently show that standard library sorts outperform average hand-written implementations because they leverage decades of low-level optimization and hardware-specific tuning that individual developers cannot easily replicate.

### Recommendation

I strongly recommend using `std::sort`. For 10 million uniformly distributed doubles, both algorithms likely exhibit similar average-case speeds since uniform distribution minimizes pivot partitioning imbalances. However, `std::sort` provides critical safety guarantees against degenerate cases and leverages extensive low-level optimizations for modern CPUs. A custom QuickSort might theoretically match performance if perfectly tuned, but this requires significant expert effort in cache-aware data structures and branch-free logic. In practical development, the risk of subtle bugs in custom implementations outweighs any marginal speedup. Standard library functions are battle-tested, portable, and maintainable. Unless you are writing a specialized real-time system with strict microsecond constraints and deep hardware knowledge, `std::sort` offers the best balance of performance, safety, and code clarity. Stick to the standard library for reliable, high-performance sorting in production environments.<|im_end|>
